brief_extract:
Sue Houlding was invited by the Meat Promotion Executive to visit Smithfield Market and talk to the experts about

Buying Beef in Bulk

Having recently bought a freezer, I thought it would be interesting to find out more about bulk buying meat for the freezer and to follow the progress of joints of meat through the wholesalers and retailers before they reach the table. I decided to take a forequarter of beef as an example as it is a cut that many people do not buy since it requires special cooking methods to get the best results, but it is the least expensive cut of beef.

brief_context: Historical figure who described Smithfield market in 1174.
brief_extract:
The meat from Smithfield is mainly sold to the retail trade in the London area, supplying the eight million or so inhabitants, as well as hotels, the tinned food industries, soap manufacturers, dog food manufacturers, and many other industries. History

The earliest mention of the market dates back to 1174 when Fitstephen, clerk to Thomas à Beckett, described the market as 'A smoothfield where every Friday there is a celebrated rendezvous of fine horses to be sold, and in another quarter are placed vendibles of the peasant, swine with their deep flanks and cows and oxen of immense bulk'. From this the site became known as 'Smoothfield' and as you can gather, livestock of all kinds was sold or slaughtered at the open market place as it was used.

Women's
Organisations
and their
Future

In a thought-provoking article Ann McMullan,
EAW Director, reflects upon the current status of
women's organisations, with an eye to their
prospects in a rapidly changing world. Over the past decade a large number of women's organisations
have been hit by the side-effects of social change.

brief_context: Quoted regarding the triumph of evil.
brief_extract:
Apathy is a social disease that is insidiously destructive. As such it
can only be overcome by determined and persistent efforts on the part
of the society it threatens, for as Edmund Burke wrote, "all that is
necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing". None of this, however, should add up to discouragement and
despondency for the many women's organisations — providing (with
less than 20 years to go before the start of the new century) they are
mindful of the absolute necessity not only to move with the times but
also to review realistically whatever changes may prove necessary or
desirable in the light of modern conditions.

You get the opportunity of doing so many things with the Board.”
She modestly comments that she regards qualifying as the main achievement of her career, but she is respected at Bridgend for her good work record, particularly for helping to build up the Board’s street lighting account. Her other achievement — gatecrashing the inviolable sanctums of a male-dominated industry — is unique, for not only is Eileen Evans the sole female engineer working for South Wales Electricity but she is also the prettiest, and is the only Board engineer who dares to list knitting as an enjoyable pastime. Engaging Speakers

There must be many Electric Living readers who belong to some sort of organisation which includes talks in its annual programme.

brief_context: Eileen Evans' husband, also an engineer with South Wales Electricity.
brief_extract:
Eileen might never have become an engineer. A desire to teach took her to a teachers' training college in Middlesex where she studied to be a music teacher — “but I got the teaching bug out of my system when I qualified as an engineer by teaching a basic engineering course at night for three years at Bridgend Technical College.”
Eileen’s friends and her husband Reg, himself a commercial engineer with South Wales Electricity, know that Eileen’s masculine job title belies her gentle character. They see her not as an oily-overalled engineer, but as a housewife with a keen interest in gardening and a talent for playing the organ at the local Christadelphian Church.

brief_extract:
A Time for Vision

Ann McMullan, EAW Director,
looks towards
the Association's Future

Electric Living will be missed by the many readers who have enjoyed its stylish and distinctive presentation of electrical information and advice. During a four-year life-span the magazine has made its mark in the electrical world with its lively contents catering regularly and specifically for a readership comprising not only EAW members themselves but also, more widely, all users of home electricity.

associated_organisation: Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust; Electrical Association for Women (EAW)
brief_context: Mentioned as the namesake of the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust.
brief_extract: Such EAW members, besides being the backbone of the Association, are also consumers whose active interest in electricity is an asset worthy of consideration. Furthermore, the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust, of which the EAW is a Trustee, is supported strongly by the membership in the important contribution it makes to electrical and general technological and scientific education. Some EAW members, and especially those who are more senior, regard these changing times with disappointment and even foreboding.
